entry.title: Examining Nondeterminism in the Futhark Programming Language
entry.content:
Links: futhark-lang.org | lobsters

The Futhark programming language blog examines the origins of nondeterminism within its parallel execution model, identifying two primary sources: language abuse through unsafe constructs like unchecked scatter operations, and floating-point roundoff errors caused by non-associative operations. While Futhark is generally characterized as a deterministic language, parallel reductions and scans alter the order of floating-point additions depending on hardware schedules, leading to replayable or approximate results.

Although fully deterministic implementations—such as tree-based summation—are possible, they incur significant performance penalties compared to hardware-optimized routines that rely on atomic instructions or backend-specific chunking. The post highlights that sacrificing strict determinism is a deliberate design choice required to maintain high performance on modern parallel hardware, balancing numerical consistency against execution speed.

entry.title: T3 Financial Crime Unit Dissolved by Crypto Giants
entry.content:
Links: bloomberg.com

The T3 Financial Crime Unit, a collaborative initiative established by Tron, Tether, Binance, and TRM Labs to combat illicit crypto activity, was quietly dissolved in August. The alliance disbanded following concerns over slow response times, despite having frozen approximately $250 million in suspicious assets during its operation.

The dissolution comes as the digital asset sector faces heightened security challenges, including major exploits and rising illicit transactions. The collapse of the joint task force highlights ongoing difficulties in coordinating rapid cross-firm responses among major cryptocurrency infrastructure providers to curb cybercrime.

entry.title: Claude Code Bug Report Reveals Account Email Exposure in User-Agent Headers
entry.content:
Links: github.com | hacker news

A bug report filed on GitHub for Anthropic's Claude Code tool reveals that the application includes users' personal account email addresses in the User-Agent HTTP request headers during automated web searches. The user who reported the issue stated that this behavior unintentionally exposes sensitive personal information to third-party websites without proper user consent or opt-out controls.

The exposed email addresses can be collected by external sites and harvested by malicious actors, resulting in increased spam and heightened privacy risks. The discussion highlights growing developer scrutiny over how agentic coding tools handle user identifiers and telemetry data during external web interactions.

entry.title: Dennis Forbes Analyzes SQLite Performance Slowdown Caused by Zig Libc Rewrite
entry.content:
Links: dennisforbes.ca | lobsters | hacker news

Developer Dennis Forbes encountered a severe performance regression when inserting large JSON datasets into SQLite via a Rust service, with operations taking minutes instead of milliseconds. The bottleneck was traced to CPU-bound string tokenization during cross-platform compilation using Zig's `cc` compiler.

The slowdown originated from a pure-Zig replacement of standard C library string functions like `strspn` within Zig's libc implementation. Unlike standard library versions, the rewritten function repeatedly measures the entire length of the string on each iteration, creating a quadratic complexity trap that dramatically degrades tokenization performance on large files.

entry.title: OpenAI Prototype Identifies and Patches Hundreds of Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities
entry.content:
Links: openai.com | hacker news

OpenAI researchers developed an autonomous pipeline to identify, validate, and patch security flaws in the Linux kernel. The prototype analyzed 2,308 candidate findings, reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and generated 948 local privilege escalation exploits and their corresponding patches.

The five-stage process—comprising discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, patch generation, and human review—is powered by specialized cyber models. This research aims to reduce the operational burden on security maintainers and increase the cost for attackers to exploit software.

entry.content:
Links: fortune.com | hacker news

Binance revealed that North Korean hackers used social engineering, including fake LinkedIn recruitment and simulated job interviews, to trick an engineer into downloading malicious software during a $6.3 billion heist. The multi-month scheme also involved an internet ad campaign promoting a tampered version of the Homebrew software package to compromise developer systems.

The combination of these exploits allowed the attackers to infiltrate internal systems, take over multiple Binance wallets, and drain funds. Although withdrawals were temporarily halted and later restored, the company recovered a portion of the stolen assets with assistance from stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle.

entry.title: The Origins and Early Development of BSD Unix
entry.content:
Links: fosscomics.com | hacker news

In the late 1970s, Bill Joy and researchers at UC Berkeley created the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) by bundling a Pascal compiler, line editors, and other utilities as an add-on package for AT&T Unix. By distributing these tools at cost, Berkeley fostered a tradition of sharing that helped spread Unix throughout universities and research institutions.

Following the release of the expanded 2BSD distribution, the acquisition of a VAX computer at Berkeley led graduate student Ozalp Babaoglu and Bill Joy to add virtual memory support to Unix 32/V. Their work culminated in 3BSD in December 1979, drawing the interest of DARPA and laying the groundwork for Unix's widespread adoption in government-funded research.

entry.title: Steal My Bitcoin Experiment Tests PHP2Shell Exploitability
entry.content:
Links: pavursec.com | lobsters | hacker news

The PHP2Shell vulnerability was tested through the "Steal My Bitcoin" experiment to determine if it was exploitable in a live environment and if AI could assist unskilled attackers. The challenge used a PHP website hosting a $500 bitcoin wallet and a binary that outputs the wallet's private key upon successful exploitation. Although one participant successfully exploited the server, the experiment found that unskilled attackers using AI were largely unsuccessful.

The experiment attracted approximately 120,000 unique visitors and generated 13 million HTTP requests. Out of 20,000 substantive attempts, only one participant successfully exfiltrated data. These results suggest that while the vulnerability is practical to exploit, the technical complexity of the attack limits success among non-experts, despite reports of its potential for widespread exploitation.

entry.title: OpenSSH on musl-based Linux Distributions Vulnerable to Password Bypass
entry.content:
Links: sshhole.com | hacker news

OpenSSH installations running on musl libc—including Alpine, OpenWrt, and Buildroot—are vulnerable to a password bypass affecting accounts with no password (marked with '*' in /etc/shadow). When a password longer than 256 characters is provided, musl's crypt() function returns '*' due to a length limit in its SHA512 implementation, which OpenSSH incorrectly validates as a successful match.

The vulnerability specifically affects systems using musl that do not utilize PAM and have password authentication enabled. To mitigate this risk, users are advised to upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or disable password authentication in their SSH configuration.

entry.title: UK Government Officials Relied on Google-Commissioned Report for £400 Billion AI Economic Claim
entry.content:
Links: wired.com

UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan disclosed in a parliamentary answer that the government's long-cited figure of £400 billion in potential economic growth from artificial intelligence originated from a 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by consultancy firm PF Global. Narayan stated that the government's current central estimate places the potential economic boost between £55 billion and £140 billion by 2030, with a central projection of £120 billion.

British government departments and agencies relied on the higher £400 billion figure for nearly two years across multiple administrations, despite internal awareness of lower projections. Critics and parliamentarians have raised concerns over the uncritical adoption of industry-funded research to shape public policy and economic forecasts, pointing to the risks of technology hype.

entry.title: Soatok Examines History of Cryptography Conspiracy Theories and NSA Standards
entry.content:
Links: soatok.blog | lobsters | hacker news

Cryptographer Soatok reviews the history of government-standardized cryptography and common conspiracy theories surrounding the National Security Agency and the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The post evaluates historical examples like DES, the Clipper Chip, and Dual_EC_DRBG to distinguish genuine security vulnerabilities from implausible paranoia.

The article highlights the tension between the NSA's dual missions in communications security and signals intelligence, discussing how historical compromises and backdoors were discovered or misunderstood by the broader cryptographic community.
